en: So how can we use HTMX to create such a
single page application-like behavior and
feeling?
Well, we could of course go to one of our
anchor elements, let's say this one here
where we load the product details, and we
could add
hx-get here, this HTMX attribute,
and then set this path here where I load the
product details as a path for hx-get so that
a GET request will be sent to this path.
Then we can also add hx-target and target
the body element so that the entire page
body will be replaced with the incoming
content.
And if we do that and we save everything
and I reload here, if I click on one of
these products,
you will see that worked.
The back button, however, does not work. It
takes me back to some other page here, which
I ran in the past.
That requested and rendered an entirely new
page, but instead we're still on the same
page as before, and it was just HTMX that
swapped the body.
And what's also great is that HTMX
automatically takes the head data of the
incoming page, like the title here, for
example, and adjusts that for the current
page.
So for example, you see that
product detail title here in the tab.
So HTMX is smart and does not try to render
the head section into the body of the
current page, which wouldn't work, but
instead it automatically grabs the body
section of the incoming page or of the
incoming response content and then
swaps that into the target we defined. And
it still takes a look at the head section to
update the title, for example. So that's a
pretty convenient behavior and that's how we
can use these attributes on this anchor
element here to build such a single page
application-like look and feel.
We still have our backend routes which
render the actual HTML content, but we then
bring them onto the screen without leaving
the page with help of HTMX.
